h: A totem pole through the floors and treasures from Cook's voyages
p: One object really does stop people in their tracks. A towering Haida totem pole from the Pacific Northwest coast of Canada rises up through the building, so you can see different parts of it from different floors. Start at the bottom and work your way up, spotting the carved figures as you climb. It's a brilliant way to get kids interested before you've even looked at a display case.

The museum has been collecting since the 1880s, and some of its most important objects came back from Captain James Cook's voyages to the Pacific in the eighteenth century. Others were gathered by Cambridge researchers on expeditions around the world. That's part of the reason the museum is so open about how things arrived here: the history of collecting is part of the story.
An hour to an hour and a half is about right for most visitors, though serious archaeology fans will happily stay longer.

Cambridge is packed with museums within easy walking distance of each other. The Museum of Zoology, also on the Downing Site, has a huge fin whale skeleton hanging over its entrance. A few minutes away on Trumpington Street, the Fitzwilliam Museum is a treasure house of art and antiquities, and the Polar Museum on Lensfield Road tells the stories of Scott, Shackleton and other polar explorers. String two or three together and you've got a fascinating rainy-day trail.
